headline: Next.js SaaS Architecture: The Patterns We Use on Every Project
description: The Next.js SaaS architecture we use: rendering strategy, multi-tenancy, RBAC, the API layer, Stripe webhooks, data access, caching, security and scaling from MVP to Series A.

itemListElement.name: Next.js SaaS Architecture: The Patterns We Use on Every Project

mainEntity.name: Is Next.js a good choice for a SaaS in 2026?

acceptedAnswer.text: For most B2B SaaS it's an excellent default: fast, SEO-friendly marketing pages and a server-rendered authenticated app in one codebase and language, with a large hiring pool. The caveats are real-time-heavy or non-web-first products, where a dedicated backend may be better.

mainEntity.name: What's the best multi-tenancy model for a Next.js SaaS?

acceptedAnswer.text: For most products, a shared database with a tenant ID on every row, enforced in the data-access layer and optionally backed by Postgres row-level security. Database-per-tenant only pays off under strict isolation or compliance needs, at higher operational cost.

mainEntity.name: Should I build my own authentication for a SaaS?

acceptedAnswer.text: No. Use a managed auth provider for identity and password storage, and own your authorization (roles and permissions) in your database, enforced server-side.

mainEntity.name: How do you handle Stripe subscriptions reliably?

acceptedAnswer.text: Treat Stripe as the source of truth and mirror subscription state into your database only via signed, idempotent webhooks, never by trusting the post-checkout client redirect. Derive entitlements from the mirrored state.
